title: Statistics - Lesson 4: Mutually Exclusive Events Practice
description: Practice identifying mutually exclusive and non-mutually exclusive events and using the correct addition rule.

questions.question: Which pair of events is mutually exclusive when one card is drawn from a standard deck?
options: Drawing a heart and drawing a spade
Drawing a red card and drawing a heart
Drawing a face card and drawing a queen
Drawing a black card and drawing a club
questions.explanation: One card cannot be both a heart and a spade because a card has only one suit.

questions.question: If two events are mutually exclusive, then P(A and B) = 0.
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so their intersection has probability 0.

questions.question: A number cube is rolled once. Let A = rolling an even number and B = rolling a number greater than 4. Which statement is correct?
options: A and B are non-mutually exclusive because 6 is in both events.
A and B are mutually exclusive because even numbers are never greater than 4.
A and B are mutually exclusive because there are two event names.
A and B are non-mutually exclusive because every number is even.
questions.explanation: A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {5, 6}. The shared outcome 6 means the events overlap.

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.35, P(B) = 0.25, and A and B are mutually exclusive, what is P(A or B)? Enter a decimal.
questions.explanation: For mutually exclusive events, add directly: 0.35 + 0.25 = 0.60.

questions.question: Why do we subtract P(A and B) in the general addition rule?
options: To correct double-counting of outcomes that are in both events
To make every probability smaller than 1/2
To remove outcomes that are impossible separately
questions.explanation: When events overlap, adding P(A) and P(B) counts the shared outcomes twice, so the overlap is subtracted once.

questions.question: In a class of 30 learners, 12 joined dance club, 10 joined drama club, and 4 joined both. How many joined dance club or drama club?
questions.explanation: Use 12 + 10 - 4 = 18. The 4 learners in both clubs should not be counted twice.

questions.question: In one sentence, explain how to decide whether two events are mutually exclusive.
questions.correctAnswer: Check whether the same outcome can belong to both events in one trial; if not, they are mutually exclusive.
questions.explanation: The key idea is whether there is a possible overlap in the same trial.

questions.question: Give one example of two non-mutually exclusive events from school life and explain why they overlap.
questions.correctAnswer: Being in the math club and being in the science club are non-mutually exclusive because one student can join both.
questions.explanation: A correct response should name two events that can happen for the same person or outcome.
